title: Localized orbitals and tunnel couplings from general confinement potentials in gate-defined quantum-dot arrays
authors: Bohdan Khromets, William Chow, Jonathan Baugh
abstract: Efficient simulation of dense gate-defined multi-quantum-dot arrays requires accurate and scalable modeling methods, compatible with asymmetries and imperfections of realistic voltage-controlled confinement potentials. We present a numerical localization procedure that rotates the eigenbasis of a general one-particle effective orbital Hamiltonian into $s$-, $p$-, $d$-, $\ldots$-shells of localized orbital wavefunctions associated with individual quantum dots. The pairwise tunnel couplings between such states are computed directly as matrix elements of the Hamiltonian. We demonstrate this procedure on a 2D triangular Si-MOS triple-quantum-dot array by obtaining the voltage dependencies of the tunnel couplings and their distributions in the presence of disorder. We discuss the implications of this evaluation method on the many-body calculations, and relate it to the experimental tunnel coupling measurements.
summary: This paper introduces a novel numerical localization procedure to accurately model single-electron physics in complex, gate-defined quantum-dot arrays. By projecting the full Hamiltonian eigenbasis onto localized orbital subspaces, the authors derive a localized basis ($\chi$-basis) and calculate tunnel couplings that are robust against disorder and potential asymmetries. This method significantly aids subsequent many-body calculations by reducing the complexity of the required Hamiltonian integrals.
main_problem: Developing accurate and scalable methods to model single-electron physics in dense, gate-defined quantum-dot arrays while accounting for realistic asymmetries and disorder.
main_result: The authors present a numerical localization procedure that successfully maps the full Hamiltonian eigenbasis onto a localized orbital basis ($\chi$-basis), allowing for the calculation of tunnel couplings across a wide dynamic range.
method: The core method involves an iterative numerical localization procedure that decomposes the full eigenbasis into orthogonal subspaces localized within defined spatial regions (dots) by solving an eigenvalue problem derived from the overlap matrix.
model_or_system: The system is a gate-defined multi-quantum-dot array, modeled using the effective-mass Hamiltonian in the conduction band landscape. The method is applied to simulate the physics of these arrays, including the effects of point defects and disorder.
key_observables: Tunnel coupling ($t$), localized orbital energies ($\epsilon(\alpha)$), and the probability distribution functions of these couplings under disorder.
important_parameters: Localization threshold ($\lambda_{thr}$), number of lowest-energy eigenstates ($M$), and the geometry/material parameters of the gate structure (e.g., $\epsilon_{	ext{SiO}_2}$, $h_{	ext{eff}}$).
main_assumptions: The initial $\psi$-states are assumed to be sufficiently smooth even in disordered potentials, and the localization procedure relies on projecting the Hamiltonian onto localized subspaces.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the localization algorithm steps, the resulting localized $\chi$-orbitals for a simulated triple-dot device, the voltage dependence of tunnel couplings, and the probability density functions of couplings in disorder.
paper_structure: The paper details the general mathematical procedure for localization, starting from the full Hamiltonian eigenbasis, defining the localized basis via an eigenvalue problem on the overlap matrix, calculating the resulting localized orbitals and tunnel couplings, and finally demonstrating the method's application to simulate disorder potentials.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general theoretical framework for simplifying complex, strongly coupled many-body problems in solid-state quantum devices by constructing a physically motivated, localized basis set.
